processing: Little is documented; the name places it in the family of Jin Jun Mei, a modern black tea developed from Lapsang Souchong methods, unsmoked.
harvest_season: Little is documented; as with Wuyi black teas of this family, spring is usual.
appearance_dry: Fine dark twisted leaf, as is typical of Wuyi black teas in this family.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden amber, as is typical of this family.
appearance_wet: Soft coppery leaf, typical of Wuyi black tea.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting description exists for this tea in particular; teas in the Jin Jun Mei family are generally sweet and soft.

brewing.notes: Slightly cooler water suits delicate Wuyi black teas of this family; go up if the cup is thin.

vintage_note: Usually sold as a recent spring harvest, like other teas in the Jin Jun Mei family. There is no agreed standard for the name, so what you get depends on the seller; ask where the leaf was grown and what it was picked as.
description:
Tong Junmei, 'copper' junmei, is a trade name that follows the pattern of Jin Jun Mei ('gold'), the well-known modern black tea from the Wuyi Mountains. Beyond that, little is documented, and it has no origin protection or published standard that is easy to point to.

What is typical of this family is unsmoked Wuyi black tea made from young leaf. How the copper grade differs in picking from its better-known relative is something to ask the seller, not to assume.

Brew it as you would a delicate black tea, with slightly cooler water and short steeps. Expect sweetness rather than smoke, and treat any confident claim about its origin with care.
history: Little is documented. The name can only be younger than Jin Jun Mei, which was itself created this century, and Tong Junmei is not among the categories of the Tongmu village black tea contest.
